title: Proper Divisors
content: **properDivisors n** = {d : 1 < d < n, d | n}. The 'interior' divisors of n, excluding the trivial divisors 1 and n. For n = 120: {2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10, 12, 15, 20, 24, 30, 40, 60} — 14 proper divisors.
mathContext: The proper divisors are the arena for the coloring game. The number of proper divisors is τ(n) - 2 (subtracting 1 and n). For the k-Egyptian property, n must have enough proper divisors with rich additive structure in their reciprocals. **Highly composite numbers** (Ramanujan, 1915) — numbers maximizing τ(n) for their size — are natural candidates. The number 120 = 2³·3·5 has 16 total divisors, 14 proper divisors, and reciprocal sum Σ 1/d ≈ 2.4 over proper divisors, making it the smallest viable candidate for k = 2.

title: k-Coloring
content: **IsColoring k S c**: a function c : ℕ → Fin k assigning one of k colors to each element. The k-Egyptian property requires that EVERY such coloring contains a monochromatic Egyptian subset.
mathContext: In **Ramsey theory**, one studies which structures are unavoidable under arbitrary colorings. The paradigmatic result is Ramsey's theorem: for any k and r, there exists N such that any k-coloring of the edges of K_N contains a monochromatic K_r. Problem #45 is a **Ramsey-type result on divisor sets**: instead of complete graphs, the underlying structure is the set of proper divisors, and instead of monochromatic cliques, we seek monochromatic subsets with reciprocal sum 1. The universality over all colorings is what makes this a Ramsey problem.

title: Monochromatic Subset
content: **IsMonochromatic c S**: all elements of S receive the same color under c. That is, ∃ color, ∀ s ∈ S, c(s) = color.
mathContext: Monochromatic subsets are the basic objects of Ramsey theory. The **pigeonhole principle** guarantees that in any k-coloring of a set of size > k·m, some color class has size > m. For Problem #45, we need not just a large monochromatic subset, but one with specific additive structure (reciprocal sum = 1). This is analogous to **Rado's theorem** on partition regularity of linear equations: a system of linear equations is partition regular if and only if it satisfies the 'columns condition'. The equation Σ 1/d_i = 1 is nonlinear, making standard Ramsey machinery insufficient.

title: Reciprocal Sum (Egyptian Fraction)
content: **reciprocalSum S** = Σ_{d ∈ S} 1/d, computed over ℚ. When this equals 1, the set S forms an **Egyptian fraction representation** of 1.
mathContext: **Egyptian fractions** express a rational number as a sum of distinct unit fractions: 1 = 1/2 + 1/3 + 1/6, or 1 = 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/6 + 1/12. The Erdős-Straus conjecture (a different problem) asks whether 4/n always has such a representation. The Rhind Papyrus (c. 1650 BCE) used Egyptian fractions extensively. For Problem #45, the key is that Egyptian fraction representations of 1 using divisors of n are constrained by the divisor structure: if d | n and d' | n, then both 1/d and 1/d' are available. Highly composite numbers n have many divisors, creating many potential representations.

title: k-Egyptian Property
content: **HasKEgyptianProperty n k**: for any k-coloring c of properDivisors(n), there exists a monochromatic subset D' with reciprocalSum D' = 1. This is a Ramsey-type property on divisor sets.
mathContext: The k-Egyptian property combines three constraints: (1) the subset D' must consist of proper divisors of n, (2) all elements of D' must share the same color, and (3) Σ_{d∈D'} 1/d = 1. The existence of n with this property is non-trivial because the coloring is adversarial: one must show that no matter how the divisors are colored, some color class contains an Egyptian representation. A **necessary condition** is that the total reciprocal sum of proper divisors exceeds k: Σ_{d | n, 1 < d < n} 1/d ≥ k. Otherwise, by pigeonhole, some color class has reciprocal sum < 1, and we could potentially color to avoid Egyptian subsets in each class.

title: Croot's Theorem (2003)
content: **croot_existence**: For all k ≥ 2, there exists n_k such that HasKEgyptianProperty n_k k. This is the main result — the k-Egyptian property is achievable. One sorry remains (the proof uses probabilistic methods).
mathContext: **Ernest Croot** proved this in his 2003 paper 'On a coloring conjecture about unit fractions'. The proof uses the **probabilistic method** (a la Erdős): take n = lcm(1, 2, ..., M) for sufficiently large M. This n has all integers up to M as divisors. The reciprocal sum of divisors is Σ_{d≤M} 1/d ≈ log M, which can be made arbitrarily large. By a careful probabilistic argument, Croot shows that for n with enough divisor structure, any k-coloring must contain a monochromatic Egyptian subset. The key insight is that the number of Egyptian representations of 1 using divisors of n grows so fast that no coloring can avoid them all.

title: Sawhney's Upper Bound
content: **sawhney_upper_bound**: The minimal n_k satisfies n_k ≤ exp(C^k) for some absolute constant C > 0. The bound is **doubly exponential** in k.
mathContext: **Mehtaab Sawhney** established the tight doubly exponential bound. The upper bound n_k ≤ exp(C^k) comes from taking n = lcm(1, 2, ..., ⌊C^k⌋). By the **prime number theorem**, lcm(1,...,N) = exp((1+o(1))N), so lcm(1,...,C^k) ≈ exp(C^k). This n has all integers up to C^k as divisors, and the proper divisor reciprocal sum is Σ_{d=2}^{C^k} 1/d ≈ k log C, which exceeds k for C large enough. The probabilistic argument then shows that for this level of 'divisor richness', the k-Egyptian property holds. The doubly exponential growth is necessary because the reciprocal sum grows only logarithmically in n.

title: Sawhney's Lower Bound
content: **sawhney_lower_bound**: If n has the k-Egyptian property, then n ≥ exp(c^k) for some constant c > 0. The doubly exponential bound is **sharp**.
mathContext: The lower bound shows that doubly exponential growth is unavoidable. The argument: for n to have the k-Egyptian property, its proper divisor reciprocal sum must satisfy Σ_{d|n, 1<d<n} 1/d ≥ k (necessary condition). By **Mertens' theorem** and the structure of σ_{-1}(n), achieving reciprocal sum ≥ k requires n to be divisible by all primes up to roughly exp(k), hence n ≥ lcm(1,...,exp(k)) ≈ exp(exp(k)). More precisely, the primes up to p satisfy Σ_{p≤x} 1/p ∼ log log x, so to get reciprocal sum ∼ k, one needs primes up to x where log log x ∼ k, giving x ∼ exp(exp(k)). This matches the upper bound up to constants.

title: Divisor Reciprocal Sum = σ_{-1}(n)
content: **divisor_reciprocal_sum**: The reciprocal sum of all divisors of n equals σ_{-1}(n) = Σ_{d|n} 1/d. This is a multiplicative function: σ_{-1}(n) = Π_{p^a || n} (1 + 1/p + ... + 1/p^a).
mathContext: The function σ_{-1}(n) = Σ_{d|n} 1/d is a special case of the **generalized divisor function** σ_s(n) = Σ_{d|n} d^s at s = -1. Being multiplicative, σ_{-1}(p^a) = (1 - 1/p^{a+1})/(1 - 1/p). For the proper divisor sum (excluding 1 and n), we get σ_{-1}(n) - 1 - 1/n. The asymptotic behavior is: the average of σ_{-1}(n) over n ≤ x is π²/6 (by Euler product), and the maximum grows as e^γ log log n + O(1) for n along primorials (Robin's theorem, related to RH).

title: Egyptian Fraction Bound (PROVED)
content: **egyptian_fraction_bound**: If D' has reciprocal sum 1 with all elements positive, then each d ∈ D' satisfies d ≤ Π_{d'∈D'} d'. **Proved by Aristotle** via `Finset.dvd_prod_of_mem` and `Nat.le_of_dvd`.
mathContext: This is a simple but useful bound: if 1 = Σ 1/d_i, multiply through by P = Π d_i to get P = Σ P/d_i. Each term P/d_i is a positive integer (since d_i | P by construction when all d_i divide some common n), so P/d_i ≥ 1 for each i, giving P ≥ |D'|. Also, each d_i | P, so d_i ≤ P. The Lean proof uses `Finset.dvd_prod_of_mem` (each element divides the product) and `Nat.le_of_dvd` (if a | b and b > 0 then a ≤ b). This was one of the lemmas **successfully proved by the Aristotle proof search system**.

title: Case k = 2: n = 120
content: **case_k_2**: 120 has the 2-Egyptian property. The number 120 = 2³·3·5 has 14 proper divisors with reciprocal sum ≈ 2.4, enough to force a monochromatic Egyptian subset under any 2-coloring.
mathContext: For k = 2, we need n with Σ_{proper d | n} 1/d ≥ 2. The number 120 = 2³·3·5 satisfies σ_{-1}(120) = (1+1/2+1/4+1/8)(1+1/3)(1+1/5) = (15/8)(4/3)(6/5) = 3, so the proper divisor sum is 3 - 1 - 1/120 ≈ 2.0. With 14 proper divisors and total reciprocal sum just over 2, any 2-coloring gives one color class with sum ≥ 1, and the Egyptian subset can be extracted greedily. Note that 120 is a **highly composite number** (Ramanujan's list), confirming the heuristic that such numbers are optimal candidates. The smallest n with the 2-Egyptian property may be even smaller than 120.
